analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes children's health insurance while barring its funds from covering parents or childless adults.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Republican leader with 19 Republican cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote; a Democratic-authored CHIP reauthorization became law about a week later.
analysis.plain_summary: The Kids First Act would have reauthorized the Children's Health Insurance Program through fiscal 2013 with steadily larger federal allotments, added $100 million a year in outreach and enrollment grants, and given states new options to cover unborn children and to subsidize private employer coverage for SCHIP-eligible children. It also would have reversed a direction several states had been taking: no new SCHIP waivers could cover parents or childless adults beyond those already enrolled, eligibility would be counted on gross income only, and federal payments for Medicaid administration would be cut 25% while provider-tax financing and special public-hospital payments were repealed.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income children on or near SCHIP eligibility, especially in states needing stable funding; community organizations doing enrollment outreach, including Indian Health Service providers and schools; parents who could use a subsidy to put an eligible child on an employer plan; and private insurers, whose employer and individual plans could receive premium-assistance dollars.

how_it_helps.text: Reauthorizes the Children's Health Insurance Program through fiscal 2013, with the national allotment rising from $7.78 billion in 2009 to $9.505 billion in 2013.
Repeals a limitation that had restricted the availability of SCHIP funding for fiscal 2008-2009, and sets new state allotments weighted toward low-income uninsured children and program spending.

Appropriates $100 million a year for outreach and enrollment grants, prioritizing areas with many eligible-but-unenrolled children, racial and ethnic minorities, and rural areas, with 10% set aside for outreach to Indian children and another 10% for a national enrollment campaign.
Gives states the option to pay a premium assistance subsidy so SCHIP-eligible children can enroll in a parent's employer plan or qualified private coverage instead of the public program.
Lets states, at their option, count an unborn child as a covered child under SCHIP and continue postpartum care for the mother through 60 days after the pregnancy ends.

analysis.who_pays: Parents and childless adults covered through SCHIP waivers, who could gain no new coverage and could lose existing coverage at their next redetermination; state budgets, through a 25% cut to Medicaid administrative payments, a flat 50% match, and repeal of provider-tax financing; and public hospitals, which lose special federal payments.

drawbacks.text: Bars any new SCHIP waiver covering parents or childless adults; only people already enrolled when the bill became law could keep coverage, at a reduced federal match, and no new enrollees could be added — so a parent of an enrolled child could lose coverage while the child stayed covered.

Requires states to set eligibility solely on gross family income, which does not net out expenses like child care; children enrolled at enactment were protected only until their next eligibility redetermination, and some could lose coverage.

Cuts federal payments for Medicaid administration by 25% and sets a flat 50% match, reducing the administrative capacity states use to enroll and keep children covered — the same populations the outreach grants are meant to reach.

Repeals the waiver of Medicaid provider tax provisions and the special federal payments for certain public hospitals, removing financing tools states and safety-net hospitals used to fund care for the poor.

The premium assistance option counts high-deductible health plans paired with health savings accounts as qualified coverage, and lets states require parents to track out-of-pocket costs and report when they hit the annual cost-sharing limit themselves.

Writes into federal statute a definition of an 'unborn child' as a member of the species Homo sapiens at any stage of development, language abortion-rights supporters object to as establishing fetal personhood in federal law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — stable SCHIP funding through 2013 and real money for outreach — was a genuine gain for low-income children, and the outreach grants with priority for rural, minority, and tribal populations were well-targeted to the problem of eligible-but-unenrolled kids. But the bill's stability came partly at others' expense: it slammed the door on new adult coverage through SCHIP, switched eligibility counting to gross income (which can push borderline families off), cut federal support for the state administration that gets children enrolled, and removed financing tools states and safety-net hospitals relied on. The premium assistance option, while framed as family-friendly, would have steered a share of children's coverage into private plans including high-deductible plans that shift costs onto families and let states offload record-keeping to parents. A family could gain a subsidized child policy through an employer while the child's parent lost waiver-based coverage under the same bill. The unborn-child provision also wrote a fetal-personhood-style definition into federal statute, which abortion-rights supporters objected to. A fair reading: a children's-coverage bill with real costs pushed onto adults, state budgets, and safety-net hospitals.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced by the Republican leader with 19 cosponsors, it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the Kids First Act on January 26, 2009; all 19 of its cosponsors were Republicans.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 without the committee reporting it out.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income children did not go without coverage: a Democratic-authored CHIP reauthorization was signed into law about a week after this bill died. Better off because this version died were states and adults relying on SCHIP waivers to cover parents and childless adults, who faced this bill's phase-out of adult coverage — though private insurers were also spared its curbs on publicly financed expansions, even as the bill would have steered more children's dollars into private plans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and adults using SCHIP waivers

for.name: Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 26, 2009, offering a Republican alternative for reauthorizing the Children's Health Insurance Program.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action; the bill never received a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Pursued its own CHIP reauthorization instead, which President Obama signed into law on February 4, 2009, less than two weeks after this bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 19 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee never acted on the bill; the CHIP reauthorization that actually became law days later was a Democratic bill.

industries.note: The premium assistance option routes SCHIP and Medicaid dollars toward employer plans and individual coverage — including high-deductible plans paired with health savings accounts — making private insurers a channel for publicly financed child coverage. At the same time the bill bars SCHIP funds from covering parents and childless adults, keeping the cheaper public program's reach narrower.

The bill repeals special federal payments to certain public hospitals that were made outside normal Medicaid disproportionate-share limits. These hospitals serve large numbers of uninsured and Medicaid patients.

States gain guaranteed, rising allotments through 2013 and outreach grants, but lose the provider-tax waiver they used to draw extra federal money, suffer a 25% cut in federal Medicaid administrative payments with a flat 50% match, and face shorter windows before unspent allotments revert to the Treasury.
